When someone mentions mental-health support, we often think supplements, therapy appointments, or devices. But your nervous system responds to free resets first.

posts.caption:
Post-COVID dysautonomia isn't rare—it's just often missed.

We're seeing more patients with postural orthostatic tachycardia (POTS) and broader autonomic dysfunction after long COVID. Most GPs aren't trained to spot it, and many patients end up frustrated and uncertain.

Functional medicine takes a different path: we investigate the root drivers—viral-immune reactivation, mast cell priming, prolonged inflammation—rather than just managing symptoms. Once we understand *why* the autonomic nervous system is dysregulated, we can rebuild resilience and actual recovery becomes possible.

If you've been struggling with persistent breathlessness, heart palpitations, brain fog, or fatigue after COVID, don't assume it's "just long COVID." Let's find out what's really happening.

Ready to explore a functional-medicine lens? Get in touch.

#LongCOVID #POTS #DysautonomiaAwareness #FunctionalMedicine #AutonomicHealth

We spend roughly a third of our lives asleep—that's far too much time for it to be biologically unimportant.

While you're sleeping, your brain is doing some of its most important work: consolidating memory, clearing metabolic waste (including proteins linked to neurodegenerative disease), and regulating hormones that govern appetite and stress.

If you're struggling with sleep quality, consistency, or both, we'd like to explore what's driving it. Often it's circadian rhythm, stress load, or nutritional deficiencies—all addressable.

HEADLINE: Anxiety isn't *just* chemicals

SUBLINE: How functional medicine reframes mental health

BODY:
Anxiety and depression are often described as simple neurotransmitter deficits. But the clinical picture is far messier—and far more hopeful—than that.

Over two decades in practice, we've noticed that mood symptoms almost always sit at the intersection of three systems: the brain's inflammation state, the gut's microbial health, and the body's nutrient reserves. A patient presenting with anxiety might be struggling with undiagnosed food sensitivities triggering systemic inflammation. Another might have depleted magnesium or iron, both of which fuel mood regulation. A third might be harbouring dysbiosis—an imbalanced microbiome that disrupts serotonin production in the gut itself.

This isn't metaphorical. The gut produces roughly 90% of the body's serotonin. Blood sugar dysregulation chronically activates the nervous system. Chronic infections or hidden inflammatory triggers can reshape how the brain processes threat. When we address these root drivers—inflammation, nutrient status, gut health—mood often shifts without a single psychiatric medication.

If you've wrestled with anxiety or depression that hasn't fully resolved despite conventional treatment, it may be time to zoom out and look at the whole system.

FOOTER: Elemental Health & Nutrition
